verses.text: After these things, when the wrath of King Ahasuerus was pacified, he remembered Vashti, and what she had done, and what was decreed against her.
Then the king’s servants who served him said, “Let beautiful young virgins be sought for the king.

Let the king appoint officers in all the provinces of his kingdom, that they may gather together all the beautiful young virgins to the citadel of Susa, to the women’s house, to the custody of Hegai the king’s eunuch, keeper of the women. Let cosmetics be given them;
and let the maiden who pleases the king be queen instead of Vashti.” The thing pleased the king, and he did so.
There was a certain Jew in the citadel of Susa, whose name was Mordecai, the son of Jair, the son of Shimei, the son of Kish, a Benjamite,
who had been carried away from Jerusalem with the captives who had been carried away with Jeconiah king of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon had carried away.

He brought up Hadassah, that is, Esther, his uncle’s daughter; for she had neither father nor mother. The maiden was fair and beautiful; and when her father and mother were dead, Mordecai took her for his own daughter.

So, when the king’s commandment and his decree was heard, and when many maidens were gathered together to the citadel of Susa, to the custody of Hegai, Esther was taken into the king’s house, to the custody of Hegai, keeper of the women.

The maiden pleased him, and she obtained kindness from him. He quickly gave her cosmetics and her portions of food, and the seven choice maidens who were to be given her out of the king’s house. He moved her and her maidens to the best place in the women’s house.
Esther had not made known her people nor her relatives, because Mordecai had instructed her that she should not make it known.
Mordecai walked every day in front of the court of the women’s house, to find out how Esther was doing, and what would become of her.

Each young woman’s turn came to go in to King Ahasuerus after her purification for twelve months (for so were the days of their purification accomplished, six months with oil of myrrh, and six months with sweet fragrances and with preparations for beautifying women).
The young woman then came to the king like this: whatever she desired was given her to go with her out of the women’s house to the king’s house.

In the evening she went, and on the next day she returned into the second women’s house, to the custody of Shaashgaz, the king’s eunuch, who kept the concubines. She came in to the king no more, unless the king delighted in her, and she was called by name.

Now when the turn of Esther, the daughter of Abihail the uncle of Mordecai, who had taken her for his daughter, came to go in to the king, she required nothing but what Hegai the king’s eunuch, the keeper of the women, advised. Esther obtained favor in the sight of all those who looked at her.
So Esther was taken to King Ahasuerus into his royal house in the tenth month, which is the month Tebeth, in the seventh year of his reign.

The king loved Esther more than all the women, and she obtained favor and kindness in his sight more than all the virgins; so that he set the royal crown on her head, and made her queen instead of Vashti.
Then the king made a great feast for all his princes and his servants, even Esther’s feast; and he proclaimed a holiday in the provinces, and gave gifts according to the king’s bounty.
When the virgins were gathered together the second time, Mordecai was sitting in the king’s gate.
Esther had not yet made known her relatives nor her people, as Mordecai had commanded her; for Esther obeyed Mordecai, like she did when she was brought up by him.
In those days, while Mordecai was sitting in the king’s gate, two of the king’s eunuchs, Bigthan and Teresh, who were doorkeepers, were angry, and sought to lay hands on the King Ahasuerus.
This thing became known to Mordecai, who informed Esther the queen; and Esther informed the king in Mordecai’s name.
When this matter was investigated, and it was found to be so, they were both hanged on a tree; and it was written in the book of the chronicles in the king’s presence.

footnotes.content: When anger cools, the heart fills with something else—sometimes yearning, sometimes regret. The king remembers Vashti not as a wife, but as an absence he created. Even in a pagan palace, I see how our choices echo back to us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in Esther's story: the exile who keeps faith in silence, the uncle who walks in prayer, the quiet acts of goodness that lay the groundwork for deliverance. We may not see God's face in this book, but we see His hand at work in faithfulness and providence—reminding us that even when we cannot see Him, He is building our salvation in the ordinary, hidden places of our lives.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The servants knew exactly what their master wanted and said it to please him. How quickly we learn to flatter and suggest, to shape our words around someone's appetite rather than toward truth. Grace teaches us a different way.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Susa was the citadel, the center of Persian power—and Hegai, keeper of the women, held a peculiar authority there. In a house built for control and beauty, the smallest kindness from a gatekeeper becomes a lifeline.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One woman to replace another, as if a heart were an office to be filled. But the Lord saw what the king's servants did not: that the quiet Jew in the citadel had a daughter the Lord loved far more than a crown.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Mordecai's family line is traced back through Shimei and Kish to a Benjamite heritage—a people with their own sorrows and histories. He carries the weight of his people even in exile, unknown in Susa. How the Lord remembers what empires forget.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Carried away with Jeconiah—Mordecai knows what exile means, what it means to be far from Jerusalem. Yet even in captivity, God had not left His people. He is with us even when we cannot see the path home.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hadassah, a myrtle tree—a girl without parents, adopted by her uncle into love and protection. Mordecai saw orphanhood and answered with belonging. In small gestures like this, I see the Father's heart toward all who are lost.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When the king's decree came, Esther went where thousands of other girls went—not by choice, but by command. She entered Hegai's house like a lamb led to an unknown place. Yet the Lord walks before those who cannot see.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hegai found favor in her, and she found it in him. In a place built for beauty and power, the first kindness she meets is from a man who sees her not as a prize but as a young woman in need of care. Small mercies are still mercies.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Mordecai's instruction: keep silent. In her silence, Esther becomes invisible—her true name, her people, her God. She keeps her heart hidden while she learns this strange new world. Faithfulness sometimes wears the face of quiet wisdom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Every day Mordecai walks in front of the court where his niece lives, asking the Lord with his feet what has become of her. This is love that will not let go, a faithfulness that will not accept distance. The Lord loves us with this kind of fierce persistence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Twelve months of preparation—myrrh and fragrances and the arts of beautifying—each girl made ready to please a king. What patience, what care went into changing a young woman into something fit for royalty. Yet the Lord sees her soul, not the oils on her skin.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One night in the king's house, and then—if not called again—she lives the rest of her life in the concubines' quarters, forgotten. How many girls entered that palace and vanished into its shadows? Yet the Lord does not forget a single tear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When Esther's turn came, she asked nothing—only took Hegai's counsel. She did not scheme or demand; she trusted. And favor rested on her like a garment. The Lord often exalts those who do not grasp.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Tebeth, the tenth month, in the seventh year of his reign—the historian marks time, the court marks seasons. Yet from heaven, the Lord marked a moment: when a quiet Jewish girl, an orphan in exile, would stand before a king's throne.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king loved her more than all the women. She became queen instead of Vashti. Yet even as the crown rested on her head, Esther knew her true crown would never rest here. The Lord had other purposes, written in a story she could not yet read.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The feast, the gifts, the holiday proclaimed—a king's joy made visible to all his empire. But joy that depends on a crown and crowds is fragile. Real joy comes from knowing we are loved by the God who needs nothing from us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The second gathering of virgins, and Mordecai sits in the king's gate—watching, waiting, his place now one of quiet authority. A man who walks in faithfulness finds his place in God's providence, even when he cannot see the whole design.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even as queen, Esther obeys Mordecai and keeps her people hidden. She does not claim her heritage or her God. There is a hidden loyalty here—to Mordecai, to her people, to the Lord—that no crown can sever.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bigthan and Teresh plot against the king—and in that moment, though no one knows it yet, a thread is laid down that will hold Mordecai's life and all his people's salvation. God works through anger, through conspiracy, through the hidden anger of doorkeepers.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Mordecai learns of the plot and tells Esther; Esther tells the king—goodness passed from hand to hand like a torch. A man does what is right, and though he does not know it, he is setting his feet on a path that will lead him to save his people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The plotters are hanged and their names written in the chronicles. But the name that matters most—Mordecai's faithfulness, his risk—is also written, though he does not yet know it will be read when his people need salvation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
